items.content:
According to Taiwan-based media outlet DigiTimes, suppliers in Taiwan, Japan, South Korea, and China are expanding production capacity for higher-margin, advanced copper-clad laminates (CCLs) in response to supply shortages, but the capacity additions are running behind schedule.

Supply-chain sources cited by DigiTimes said Taiwan’s Elite Material Co. (EMC) and South Korea’s Doosan Corporation Electro-Materials BG have each seen their CCL equipment installation schedules delayed by about six months. Construction delays were cited as the cause at EMC, while Doosan’s delay followed a workplace safety incident at a construction site.

Taiwan Union Technology (TUC) has also experienced delays. Equipment delivery problems in the second quarter of 2026 pushed back mass production for the second phase of its Thailand plant by roughly two months. Nevertheless, production began in July, with shipments expected to increase from August as the plant ramps up.

These delays suggest that high-end CCL shortages and extended lead times are unlikely to ease in the near term.

Production capacity for AI server PCB-grade CCL remains concentrated among a small group of Tier 1 suppliers, including Taiwan’s EMC, TUC, and Nan Ya Plastics; Japan’s Panasonic Industry; South Korea’s Doosan; and China’s Shengyi Technology. With upstream material supplies also tight, lead times for high-end CCL have reportedly stretched to four to six months.

Supply-chain sources expect Doosan to be the sole supplier of CCL for compute boards during the initial production ramp of Nvidia’s Vera Rubin server platform. Meanwhile, Nan Ya is expected to join Shengyi and EMC in supplying materials for Vera Rubin switch boards.
— Jukan (@jukan05) Aug 20, 2026

items.content:
Samsung Electronics Accelerates Taylor Fab 2 Buildout, Asks Equipment Suppliers to Secure Certifications in Advance

Samsung Electronics is accelerating efforts to expand its advanced foundry capacity in the United States. Ahead of the planned groundbreaking for the second Taylor fab at the end of this year, the company has recently begun preemptively pursuing certifications required to introduce equipment from its suppliers.

According to industry sources on August 20, Samsung Electronics has asked key suppliers to obtain the certifications necessary to supply equipment for investment in the second Taylor foundry fab.

The Taylor facility will be dedicated to mass production using Samsung Electronics’ most advanced foundry technologies. Equipment is currently being moved into and installed at the first fab, which is scheduled to begin operations by the end of this year. Its primary production target is the industry-leading 2-nanometer process, with Tesla, a major U.S. technology company, widely cited as a key customer.

Samsung Electronics recently also formalized its plan to begin construction of the second Taylor fab. During its second-quarter earnings conference call on July 30, the company said, “To respond to growing customer demand in a timely manner, we are preparing to begin construction of the second Taylor fab by the end of this year, with mass production targeted for 2030.”

Samsung Electronics is believed to be demonstrating a strong commitment to investing in the second Taylor fab. The company has recently asked multiple semiconductor equipment suppliers to obtain “SEMI” certification in advance so their equipment can be installed at the facility. SEMI certification is a standard used to assess the safety of semiconductor equipment and must be secured before the equipment can be shipped overseas.

“Although the detailed specifications for the second Taylor fab have not yet been finalized, Samsung Electronics’ Foundry Business has begun responding more quickly than expected,” an official from the semiconductor equipment industry said. “Specific plans are expected to become clearer toward the end of this year, but the early action suggests that Samsung is actively preparing for the investment.”

The key issue is whether Samsung can secure major customers for its leading-edge processes. Samsung Electronics previously postponed its investment plans for the first Taylor fab several times due to difficulties securing customers during the initial phase of construction and a deterioration in market conditions. However, construction regained momentum after Tesla signed a KRW 22.76 trillion semiconductor contract-manufacturing agreement with Samsung Foundry in the third quarter of last year.

The roadmap for bringing the second Taylor fab into commercial production is likewise expected to depend on whether it is used to expand supply to Tesla or whether Samsung secures additional customers.

“I understand that Samsung E&A, Samsung’s engineering and construction affiliate, is also considering dispatching dozens of employees to the site to support construction of the second Taylor facility,” a semiconductor industry official said. “However, for Samsung Electronics to move swiftly from cleanroom construction to the installation of an actual mass-production line, it will first need to secure a major customer.”

items.content:
Korean media report that Samsung plans to increase the number of floors at its new fab under construction in Pyeongtaek from the originally planned two to three.

More specifically, the fabs being redesigned as three-story facilities are Pyeongtaek P5 Plants 1 and 2, which together will constitute the world’s largest semiconductor manufacturing facility at a single site. Construction first began in 2022, with final completion targeted for 2030. At peak construction, the site has employed as many as 50,000 workers.

Up through P4, which recently began operations at Samsung Electronics’ Pyeongtaek campus, each building employed a double-fab configuration with four cleanrooms. If the revised plan is approved, however, P5 will adopt a triple-fab configuration accommodating up to six cleanrooms. With the number of cleanrooms increasing by 50%, production capacity is also expected to rise by at least 50%.

Future semiconductor fabs to be built by Samsung Electronics and SK hynix in the national and general industrial complexes planned for Yongin are also expected to adopt this triple-fab configuration.

items.content:
SK hynix to Accelerate KRW 40 Trillion Share Buyback and Cancellation; Raises Shareholder Return Target to “At Least 50% of FCF”

▶️ Share Buyback and Cancellation

- On August 19, the board approved the repurchase and cancellation of KRW 40 trillion worth of treasury shares.

- Based on the previous day’s closing price of KRW 1,662,000 per share, the company plans to acquire approximately 24.07 million shares, equivalent to around 3.3% of total shares outstanding.

- The repurchase will begin on August 20 and continue for approximately three months, after which all acquired shares will be cancelled.

- This will be the largest share cancellation ever undertaken by a Korean-listed company.

▶️ Rationale Behind the Decision

- The company believes its current share price does not adequately reflect its intrinsic value, considering its business competitiveness, cash-generating capacity, and medium- to long-term growth prospects.

- SK hynix’s net cash position reached approximately KRW 69 trillion as of the end of the second quarter, reflecting a significant improvement in cash generation.

▶️ Accelerated Implementation of Shareholder Return Policy

- The company is accelerating the implementation of its existing policy to return up to 50% of cumulative free cash flow generated between 2025 and 2027.
It also plans to raise its shareholder return target from “up to 50% of cumulative FCF” to “at least 50%.”

- With progress toward its financial soundness targets remaining on track, the company intends to continue shareholder returns while maintaining a stable financial structure.

▶️ Next Steps

- SK hynix plans to combine share buybacks and cancellations with cash dividends, while also considering measures to expand dividends, including higher fixed dividends and special dividends.

- The specific size and structure of additional shareholder returns will be determined by the board and announced alongside the company’s third-quarter earnings results.

items.content:
Taiwanese media reported that the PCB industry has continued to raise prices as supplies of raw materials such as CCL and prepreg (PP) tighten and costs increase.

PCB makers have already raised quoted prices by approximately 5–30% this year, with the benefits of those increases gradually being reflected from the third quarter onward.

With upstream material prices remaining elevated, PCB manufacturers are preparing further price increases in the second half through dynamic pricing adjustments to mitigate the erosion of gross margins caused by rising raw material costs.

The main driver of PCB price increases is the broad-based rise in upstream material prices.

Major CCL manufacturers raised product prices by approximately 20–30% in the first half of this year, and quarter-by-quarter pricing pressure is expected to persist from the second half through 2027.

Supplies of high-end electronic-grade glass fiber fabric are also tight. The supply-demand shortfall for second-generation Low Dk fabric is estimated to exceed 60%, while the shortage of T-Glass continues to widen. Prices of high-end glass fiber fabric could continue rising through the first half of 2027.

Meanwhile, the price-increase trend is also continuing in the IC substrate market in the second half. As demand for high-performance computing applications such as AI GPUs and ASICs grows—and supplies of advanced materials, including T-Glass, remain tight—substrate manufacturers are continuing to adjust prices on a rolling basis. Quoted prices are reportedly considered to have room for double-digit increases in each of the third and fourth quarters.

items.content:
AI Server Demand Drives Polarization in MLCC Lead Times, With High-End Products Approaching 10 Months

Korean media reports that MLCC lead times are diverging sharply depending on product specifications.

While supply conditions for general-purpose products remain relatively stable, lead times for high-capacitance, high-end products used in artificial intelligence servers have lengthened significantly.

According to TTI’s lead-time trend chart, as of August, lead times for most standard case-size multilayer ceramic capacitors remain at 14–18 weeks, or approximately 3.5–4.5 months. High-capacitance and high-voltage products have lead times of around 15–20 weeks, or roughly 4–5 months.

Avnet Abacus’s August 2026 lead-time guide similarly lists multilayer surface-mount, high-capacitance, and automotive-grade products at eight to more than 20 weeks, or approximately 2–5 months, with the outlook categorized as stable.

The situation is different for high-end products.

ComponentNews classifies server-grade MLCCs as being at a critical supply level, with lead times of more than 20 weeks—or over five months—for Murata and Samsung Electro-Mechanics products. It expects these conditions to persist through the second half of this year.

DigiKey’s lead-time data also shows significant supplier-to-supplier variation in high-capacitance products, with some Samsung Electro-Mechanics components averaging around 40 weeks. Lead times for Murata’s high-capacitance products of 1 microfarad or more reached as much as 30 weeks in July, up from 24 weeks in June. Some distribution channels have cited lead times of up to 36 weeks.

The main driver of this polarization is surging demand from AI servers and data centers. AI servers require five to 13 times more high-capacitance, compact, and highly reliable MLCCs than conventional servers for power-delivery-network decoupling and filtering.

Korean media emphasizes that lead times of five to more than 10 months for high-end products are likely to persist for the foreseeable future. Unlike in the past, when passive-component lead times moved flexibly with the economic cycle, the current pronounced divergence is being interpreted not as a temporary boom but as a fundamental restructuring of demand centered on AI.

Moreover, new capacity expansions have been pushed back from the fourth quarter of 2026 into 2027, making it difficult to resolve the supply-demand imbalance in the near term. Major manufacturers are simultaneously raising prices and entering into more long-term supply agreements.

Lead times exceeding five months and approaching a full year indicate that manufacturers have reached a point where they cannot quickly increase supply. At the same time, they signal strengthening pricing power and the beginning of a meaningful improvement in profitability driven by a richer mix of high-value products.
— Jukan (@jukan05) Aug 18, 2026

items.content:
Korean media reports that TSMC has secured a technological edge in backside power delivery with A16, putting it a step ahead of Intel and Samsung in the competition.

Specifically, TSMC has successfully developed and validated A16, the industry’s first angstrom-class CMOS platform featuring its Super Power Rail (SPR) backside power delivery scheme.

The key achievement is that A16 retains the gate density and design flexibility enabled by NanoFlex in the existing N2P process, an enhanced version of N2.

In conventional semiconductor chips, both power-delivery interconnects and signal interconnects are placed together on the front side of the chip. As process nodes shrink, however, competition between the two in an increasingly confined space exacerbates routing congestion and increases electrical resistance, leading to more severe voltage-drop, or IR-drop, problems.

Addressing these issues through backside power delivery typically requires substantial changes to transistor placement or cell structures.

These challenges become more pronounced as process nodes shrink. Supplying power from the back side of the chip has generally required designers to give up parts of their existing cell libraries and design expertise.

TSMC has completely separated the power-delivery network from the front-side signal wiring by moving it to the back side of the chip. Power is delivered directly to the source and drain of each transistor through dedicated vertical connections, or VBs. In the process, TSMC has kept the front-side gate structure, cell dimensions, and layout area almost unchanged, preserving compatibility with existing designs.

Intel, by contrast, had already modified its existing cell configuration and redesigned its cell architecture during PowerVia testing, including adjustments to pin counts and the relaxation of metal-pitch requirements. Samsung Electronics is also reportedly working to introduce backside power delivery with its SF2 process, but is said to be likely to pursue an approach similar to Intel’s.

TSMC’s achievement is viewed as a technology that can improve efficiency while reducing design complexity for products such as AI accelerators, which require both high power efficiency and strong performance.
